content: People who use nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including salsalate (but excluding aspirin), may face an increased risk of heart attack or stroke compared to those who do not use these medications. These cardiovascular events can occur suddenly and may be fatal. The risk is particularly elevated in individuals who use NSAIDs for extended periods. Inform your doctor if you or your family members have a history of heart disease, heart failure, heart attack, or stroke. Seek immediate medical attention if you experience symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side of the body, or slurred speech. If you are scheduled for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, do not take salsalate immediately before or after the procedure. NSAIDs like salsalate can also lead to ulcers, bleeding, or perforations in the stomach or intestines. These complications can arise at any time during treatment, often without warning, and may be life-threatening. The risk is higher in individuals who use NSAIDs long-term, are older, have poor overall health, smoke, or consume large amounts of alcohol while taking salsalate. Notify your doctor if you are taking medications such as anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), aspirin, other NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen), or oral steroids (e.g., dexamethasone, methylprednisolone, prednisone). Also, inform your doctor if you have a history of ulcers, gastrointestinal bleeding, or other bleeding disorders. If you experience symptoms such as stomach pain, heartburn, vomiting blood or material resembling coffee grounds, blood in the stool, or black, tarry stools, stop taking salsalate and contact your doctor immediately. Regularly attend all medical and laboratory appointments, as your doctor will monitor your symptoms and may order tests to evaluate your response to the medication. Your doctor or pharmacist will provide you with a Medication Guide from the manufacturer when you start salsalate and each time you refill your prescription. Read this information carefully and ask any questions you may have. You can also access the Medication Guide on the FDA or manufacturer’s website. Salsalate is prescribed to alleviate pain, tenderness, swelling, and stiffness associated with rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and other inflammatory conditions. It belongs to the salicylate class of NSAIDs and works by inhibiting the production of substances in the body that cause pain, fever, and inflammation. Salsalate is available in tablet form and is typically taken two to three times daily. To reduce the risk of stomach upset, it can be taken with food or milk. Take the medication at the same times each day, following the instructions on your prescription label. Do not take more or less than prescribed. It may take three to four days to experience the full benefits of salsalate. If your symptoms worsen or do not improve, contact your doctor. Before taking salsalate, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to salsalate, aspirin, other NSAIDs, or any of the ingredients in the medication. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking or plan to take. This includes medications such as acetazolamide, ACE inhibitors, antacids, diuretics, lithium, gout medications, diabetes medications, seizure medications, methotrexate, penicillin, salicylates, and thyroid medications. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have a history of asthma (especially with nasal polyps or frequent nasal congestion), gout, kidney or liver disease, or swelling in the extremities. Salsalate should not be given to children or teenagers with chickenpox, flu, or recent varicella vaccination due to the risk of Reye’s syndrome. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking salsalate, notify your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures, inform your healthcare provider that you are taking salsalate. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking salsalate. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Salsalate may cause mild side effects such as diarrhea or dizziness. Notify your doctor if these symptoms persist or worsen. Serious side effects include ringing in the ears, hearing loss, difficulty breathing or swallowing, shortness of breath, hoarseness, rapid heartbeat, unexplained weight gain, swelling, rash, hives, blisters, itching, unusual bleeding or bruising, pale or cold skin, fever, nausea, headache, extreme fatigue, weakness, loss of appetite, upper right abdominal pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, flu-like symptoms, discolored or bloody urine, back pain, or painful urination. If you experience any of these, contact your doctor immediately. Report any unusual side effects to your doctor or the FDA’s MedWatch program. Store salsalate in its original container, tightly sealed, at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Keep it out of reach of children. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, consulting your pharmacist if needed. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual has collapsed or is not breathing. Symptoms of overdose may include ringing in the ears, dizziness, headache, confusion, extreme fatigue, sweating, rapid breathing, intense thirst, muscle cramps, fainting, flushing, or loss of consciousness. Before undergoing any laboratory tests, inform the healthcare provider that you are taking salsalate. Do not share this medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
